summary: Defines a Management Information Base module with textual conventions for representing floating-point numbers in SNMP management data.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP's number types only cover whole numbers. This adds definitions so monitoring tools can store numbers with decimal points, like 3.14.

questions: how are floating point numbers represented in snmp
what is a textual convention in a mib
subtitle: Three ready-made SNMP data types for carrying 32-, 64- and 128-bit IEEE floating-point numbers.

tldr.problem: Network management data had no standard way to represent floating-point numbers, even though 32-bit, 64-bit and 128-bit IEEE formats were recognized as needed.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module with three textual conventions, Float32TC, Float64TC and Float128TC, each an OCTET STRING of 4, 8 or 16 octets holding an IEEE 754-2008 binary interchange value.
tldr.outcome: MIB designers can reuse these types instead of inventing their own, though the text warns that floating point is often the wrong choice and that INDEX ordering and range limits need care.

today: RFC 6340 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2011. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Floating-Point Types Were Needed
sections.content:
RFC 6340 defines textual conventions (TCs) for representing floating-point numbers in a Management Information Base (MIB) module. All of them are defined in terms of the IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic, IEEE 754-2008.

That standard provides a variety of interchange formats. The memo says three of them have been recognized as needed in network management: 32-bit, 64-bit and 128-bit. It points to Section 4.2.3 of the SMIng Objectives (RFC 3216) as an example of that need.

The text also notes that choosing a floating-point format involves many considerations and trade-offs, and refers readers to Knuth and to Goldberg for background on the fundamentals and on the IEEE formats.
sections.plainLanguage: People who watch networks sometimes need numbers with decimals. Three sizes of number box were found useful, so this memo makes one standard box of each size.

sections.title: The Management Framework Context
sections.content:
Managed objects live in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB). MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and they are defined with the Structure of Management Information (SMI).

This memo specifies a MIB module compliant with SMIv2, described in STD 58 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580). For an overview of the whole framework it points to RFC 3410.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices keep a big list of facts about themselves, and a standard language describes what each fact looks like. This memo adds a few new kinds of fact to that language.

sections.title: The Three Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module, FLOAT-TC-MIB, defines three textual conventions and no MIB objects. Each one is an OCTET STRING of a fixed size:

  • Float32TC: a 32-bit (4-octet) IEEE floating-point number.
  • Float64TC: a 64-bit (8-octet) IEEE floating-point number.
  • Float128TC: a 128-bit (16-octet) IEEE floating-point number.

All three use the binary interchange format of IEEE 754-2008. The highest-order bit of the first byte is the sign bit, and the remaining bits of the octet string hold the exponent and fraction parts, in network byte order. The module imports definitions from RFC 2578 and RFC 2579, and its REFERENCE clauses point to IEEE 754-2008.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three boxes: a 4-byte box, an 8-byte box and a 16-byte box. The first bit in each says plus or minus, and the rest holds the number's digits in a fixed order.

sections.title: Applicability and Cautions
sections.content:
Section 3 gives MIB designers a checklist of issues to weigh before using these types:

  • Floating point suits a large dynamic range. For a limited range, fixed-point numbers can be more efficient and more precise, and truly decimal data is often better handled by changing units and using scaled integers.
  • Used as an INDEX, the SNMP lexicographic ordering follows the octet strings, which will not always match numeric order. A walk of the table may surprise users, so the DESCRIPTION clause should carry a warning.
  • Embedded systems sometimes lack floating-point support, which complicates implementation.
  • Pick the type for the range and precision needed. Using Float128TC where Float64TC would do could be inefficient.
  • Because the types are OCTET STRING, the SMI cannot set formal range constraints. Designers must state any extra range limits in DESCRIPTION clauses.
  • The DESCRIPTION must say whether denormalized numbers, NaNs ("not a number") or infinities are permitted and what they mean. This matters most for writeable objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says: do not use a decimal box if a whole number will do, and do not pick the biggest box if a smaller one is enough. Also, sorting these boxes by their bytes may not put the numbers in the right order.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The module defines no management objects, only conventions that other MIB modules can use. The memo therefore says meaningful security considerations can only be written in the MIB modules that define objects, and that it has no impact on the security of the Internet.

For IANA, the module's identifier floatTcMIB is recorded in the SMI Numbers registry as { mib-2 201 }.
sections.plainLanguage: These are just labels for boxes, so they cannot be dangerous on their own. Whoever uses a box in a real list has to think about safety there.
